overview:
For roughly three thousand years a single river valley sustained one of the ancient world's most durable states. Unification of the Nile valley and Delta around 3000 BCE produced a kingdom whose wealth came from the river's annual flood, whose ideology fused kingship with the divine order, and whose bureaucracy learned early to write, survey land, and store grain. That state moved through long cycles — the pyramid-building Old Kingdom, the reconsolidation of the Middle Kingdom, the imperial New Kingdom that pushed armies into Nubia and Syria — separated by intermediate periods when central authority fractured. Egyptians themselves understood their history as a sequence of dynasties, a framework inherited from the priest Manetho and still, with heavy modification, the one Egyptology uses.

By the seventh and sixth centuries BCE, Egypt was no longer the region's dominant power but one player among several in a crowded Near East. The Saite kings of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, ruling from Sais in the Delta from 664 BCE, rebuilt a unified and prosperous state, hired Greek and Carian mercenaries, expanded trade, and deliberately revived the art and script of far older periods. Their foreign policy pulled them north. When the Neo-Assyrian Empire collapsed under Babylonian and Median pressure, Necho II marched to prop up its remnants, killing King Josiah of Judah at Megiddo on the way. The reckoning came at Carchemish on the Euphrates, where Nebuchadnezzar, then Babylonian crown prince, destroyed the Egyptian and Assyrian force. Egypt withdrew from Syria and the Levant for good, though Necho did halt a Babylonian thrust at the Egyptian frontier a few years later, and Egypt itself was not invaded.

What followed was a long sequence of conquests interrupted by native revivals: Persian rule from Cambyses II's victory at Pelusium in 525 BCE, a period of restored independence in the fourth century, a second Persian occupation, then Alexander in 332 BCE and three centuries of Macedonian Ptolemaic rule from Alexandria. The line the dataset draws at 29 BCE marks the end of that last dynasty, when Cleopatra VII's defeat left Egypt a province of Rome — though pharaonic temple building, hieroglyphic writing, and Egyptian religion continued for centuries afterward under Roman emperors who had themselves carved on the walls as kings of Upper and Lower Egypt.
significance: Egypt supplied much of the ancient Mediterranean's working vocabulary for monumental architecture, state administration, sculpture, and the afterlife, and its grain later fed Rome. Just as important is what the dry climate preserved: papyri, painted tombs, mummified bodies, and administrative records that let historians reconstruct ordinary lives — wages, lawsuits, letters home — at a resolution almost no other ancient society allows. The country's long entanglement with Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome also makes it a hinge for dating the rest of the ancient Near East, and its rediscovery after Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822 helped create archaeology as a discipline, along with a durable and often distorting European fascination with things Egyptian.
coverage: Written from encyclopedia-level reference works on Egypt and its Late Period plus targeted reading on Carchemish; the dataset itself holds only that one event, so the overview sketches three millennia the map does not yet illustrate. Two gaps worth naming: Carchemish is dated here to 604 BCE, whereas the Babylonian Chronicle places the fighting around May–June 605 BCE and most scholarship follows it, and the battle is known only from Babylonian and biblical sources — no Egyptian account survives, so Necho's losses come to us entirely from the winners and their allies. More broadly, dates before about 700 BCE carry error bars of decades or more, and the surviving record everywhere favors kings, priests, and the literate over almost everyone else.
